'''''Veronica persica''''' is a [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Plantaginaceae]]. Common names include '''birdeye speedwell''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=VEPE3|taxon=Veronica persica|access-date=29 July 2015}}</ref> '''common field-speedwell''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref> '''Persian speedwell''', '''large field speedwell''', '''bird's-eye''', or '''winter speedwell'''. The most widespread species of ''[[Veronica (genus)|Veronica]],'' it is native to [[West Asia|western Asia]] but has been introduced worldwide.<ref name=":1" />

==Description==
''Veronica persica'' is an annual that reproduces from seed.

Its [[cotyledon]]s are triangular with truncated bases. The short-stalked leaves are broadly ovate with coarsely serrated margins, and measure {{convert|1|to|2|cm|spell=in|1}} long. The leaves are paired on the lower stem and are alternately arranged on the upper parts. The plant has weak stems that form a dense, prostrate [[groundcover]]. The tips of stems often grow upright.

The flowers are roughly {{convert|1|cm|spell=in|1}} wide<ref name="Rhoads">Rhoads, A. F. and T. A. Block. ''Plants of Pennsylvania: An Illustrated Manual'', 2nd ed. University of Pennsylvania Press, Philadelphia. 2007.</ref> and are sky-blue with dark stripes and white centers. They are [[zygomorphic]], having only one vertical plane of symmetry. They are solitary on long, slender, hairy stalks in the [[Wiktionary:axil|leaf axil]]s.

The seeds are transversely rugose and measure between {{convert|1|and|2|mm|spell=in|2}} long. There are five to 10 seeds per [[locule]] in the fruit.<ref name="Gleason">Gleason, H. A. and A. Cronquist. ''Manual of Vascular Plants of Northeastern United States and Adjacent Canada'', 2nd ed. New York Botanical Gardens, New York, New York. 1991.</ref>

Similar species include ''Veronica persica'' fruit, which have lobes that widely diverge to form a spreading 'V', and solitary flowers emerging from the stem with the leaf stalks, whilst the flower stalks are regularly much longer than the leaves. Other similar species include ''[[Veronica polita]]'' and ''[[Veronica agrestis]]'' (whose fruit lobes are parallel and flower stalks are shorter than or equal to the leaves), ''[[Veronica crista-galli]]'' (whose flowers and fruits are smaller than the calyx, and the calyx is formed of two bilobed parts not four unlobed parts), ''[[Veronica filiformis]]'' (whose small round leaves are smaller than or equal to the flowers, ''[[Veronica chamaedrys]]'' and ''[[Veronica montana]]'' (whose flowers are not solitary but form short unleafy spikes of flowers), and ''[[Veronica hederifolia]]'' (whose flowers are small and leaf lobing has a different appearance).<ref name="Sell3">{{cite book |title=Flora of Great Britain and Ireland, vol. 3, p. 464-474 |author=Peter Sell & Gina Murrell}}</ref>

== Taxonomy ==
''Veronica persica'' was given its scientific name in 1808 by the botanist [[Jean Louis Marie Poiret]]. It is classified in the genus [[Veronica (plant)|''veronica'']] within the [[Plantaginaceae]] family.<ref name="POWO" /> The spices is generally considered to be an [[Allopolyploid|allotetraploid]] species that arose via a [[Hybridisation (biology)|hybridisation]] event. Based on morphological, cytological and chemical evidence, Fischer (1987) proposed that the species originated through hybridization between the diploid species ''[[Veronica polita]]'' and ''[[Veronica ceratocarpa]]'', followed by genome duplication.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Fischer |first=Manfred A. |date=1987-03-01 |title=On the origin ofVeronica persica (Scrophulariaceae)—a contribution to the history of a neophytic weed |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00936294 |journal=Plant Systematics and Evolution |language=en |volume=155 |issue=1 |pages=105–132 |doi=10.1007/BF00936294 |issn=1615-6110}}</ref> The species has morphological traits which are intermediate between the traits of the two proposed ancestral species, including fruit size and [[sepal]] length. Its [[Ploidy|chromosome number]] (28) is double that of ''V. polita'' and ''V. ceratocarpa'' (14). This interpretation is cited elsewhere,<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Veronica persica Poir. |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/3172077 |access-date=2026-03-28 |website=www.gbif.org |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{cite web 
 |title=Veronica persica Poir. 
 |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.5p6 
 |publisher=Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland 
 |website=BSBI Online Plant Atlas 2020 
 |year=2020 
 |access-date=28 March 2026
}}</ref> but has not yet been fully confirmed using modern genomic data.

''Veronica persica'' has several [[Variety (botany)|varieties]] among its 31 [[Synonym (botany)|synonyms]] and also {{table row counter|id=Synonyms}} species.<ref name="POWO">{{Cite POWO |last1=POWO |date=2026 |id=30198355-2 |title=''Veronica persica'' Poir. |access-date=22 April 2026}}</ref>

== Distribution ==
''Veronica persica'' is native to the [[Caucasus]] and [[northern Iran]], but it has become widely naturalised elsewhere.<ref name=":2">{{cite POWO 
 |id=urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:30198355-2 
 |title=Veronica persica 
 |access-date=28 March 2026
}}</ref> It now has a near [[Cosmopolitan distribution|cosmopolitan]] distribution,<ref name=":1" /> having been introduced to [[Europe]], [[North Africa]], [[Americas|the Americas]], [[East Asia]], [[Australia]] and [[New Zealand]].<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":0" />

The species was first recorded in Britain in 1825.<ref name="Blamey">Blamey, M., et al. 2003. ''Wild flowers of Britain and Ireland: The Complete Guide to the British and Irish Flora.'' A & C Black, London.</ref> It rapidly extended its range during the 1800s and was ubiquitous throughout lowland Britain and Ireland by 1960.<ref name=":0" />

==Ecology==
''Veronica persica'' is a common [[Ruderal species|ruderal]] and arable [[weed]] associated with disturbed habitats such as [[Field (agriculture)|cultivated fields]], gardens, lawns and roadsides. The plant prefers moist conditions and grows well in loamy, nutrient-rich soil.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bird's Eye Speedwell (''Veronica persica'') |url=https://www.illinoiswildflowers.info/weeds/plants/be_speedwell.htm |access-date=17 May 2022 |website=Illinois Wildflowers}}</ref> It is self-compatible and produces many seeds. It can germinate and flower throughout the year, and can spread vegetatively from stem fragments.<ref name=":0" /> These traits have contributed to the species' success outside its native range. Its seeds may be dispersed by ants.<ref>{{cite web
 |title=Distribution and biology of common field speedwell
 |url=https://ahdb.org.uk/knowledge-library/distribution-and-biology-of-common-field-speedwell-in-the-uk
 |publisher=Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board
 |website=AHDB Knowledge Library
 |access-date=28 March 2026
}}</ref>

== Horticultural uses ==
Although many species in the genus are used in gardens (such as ''[[Veronica exalta|V. exalta]]'', ''[[Veronica incana|V. incana]]'', ''[[Veronica gentianoides|V. gentianoides]]'', ''[[Veronica longifolia|V. longifolia]]'', ''[[Veronica perfoliata|V. perfoliata]]'', and ''[[Veronica spicata|V. spicata]]''),<ref name="Thomas">Thomas, G. S. ''Perennial Garden Plants or the Modern Florilegium'', 2nd ed. J. M. Dent and Sons, London. 1992.</ref> this species is generally seen as a weed<ref name=usda>[https://plants.usda.gov/java/profile?symbol=VEPE3&photoID=vepe3_003_ahp.tif ''Veronica persica''.] USDA Plants Database.</ref> and has no known horticultural uses.

==Herbal medicine==
Afghani [[herbalist]] [[Mahomet Allum]] used the plant to treat patients with heart trouble, in [[Adelaide]], Australia, in the mid-20th century.<ref name=RG>{{cite thesis |title=Historical Archaeology Report: Mahomet Allum Khan |date=2018 |doi=10.13140/RG.2.2.23125.27365 |author1=Amirul Husni Affifudin }}</ref>{{unreliable source?|date=March 2021}}
